segments.description: Coaches, our next presenter is Mark Tannert. Mark has over 30 years experience coaching in clubs and tennis centers in the UK. He has been training coaches for the LTA and ITF for over 20 years and has tutored more than 100 certification courses for the LTA. Mark was a lead member of the team, charged with the development and launch of the ITF Tannerts program play and stay campaign, working with staff and experts from other major nations. This also involved writing the ITF Tannerts play and stay manual, which has been translated into over 30 languages and the ITF adults tennis program Tannerts Express. Mark is a regular speaker at conferences worldwide and has presented on every continent, both in English and French. Mark is a founder and director of Inspire2Coach, a company that offers coach education worldwide and runs more than 30 tennis facilities in the UK. As an LTA coach development center, Inspire2Coach has so far certified over 10,000 coaches and assistants in the UK. Today, Mark is here to share some of his insights into the youth development of kids. Please welcome Mark. Hi, my name is Mark Tannert and it's my great pleasure to join you today to give this short presentation. Did you know that research shows that the average child of 2015 would have finished 250 meters behind the average child from the 1980s when measured over a 1.6 kilometer run? Or that the least fit children from 20 years ago

And as a Brit, whilst it pains me to say it, Australia rightly prides itself on being a sporting nation, but Australia is also one of the world's most overweight nations with around two thirds of adults and a quarter of children either overweight or obese. In an increasingly sedentary world, which is driven so much by technology, at our fingertips, we know that a lot of children are spending increasing amounts of time in front of their screens. And the stats tell us that at nine to 11 years old, the average is around two hours per day, increasing to around three hours per day in our late teens. However, we also know that habits are formed at an early stage, and I'll talk about this a little bit more in a moment. And a study from the US tells us that around about 73% of adults who play sport participated when they were younger. So if we can catch them young and we do a good job, then there's no reason why we shouldn't keep them in sport. And this means that they build the habit of physical activity early and are then reaping the rewards in adulthood. I'm sure you're aware of a lot of the health benefits of physical activity, especially applied to tennis, but I've listed a few here just for clarity. We know that exercise and tennis in particular is good as a fight against obesity and being overweight. We know that tennis is good for the heart and it's good for the bones, the muscles, the ligaments and tendons.
